title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
gist: The FCC voted to let state and local prisons jam contraband cellphones for the first time, carving an exception to a 90-year non-federal jamming ban, while CTIA and AT&T say pilot data shows jammers block 911 and lawful calls up to 2.5 miles away yet miss half to two-thirds of contraband calls. The order is a likely court target and opens a new US market for jamming equipment and prison-telecom vendors.

insights.claim: The FCC voted to authorize state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cellphones for the first time, creating an exception to the Communications Act-based prohibition on non-federal jamming.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Opens a newly legal US market for prison micro-jamming systems and associated vendors.
insights.quote: Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time
insights.locator: The FCC approved the jamming order

insights.claim: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr says jamming technology has advanced enough to be focused with geographic precision, and no correctional facility will be required to deploy it.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Adoption will be voluntary and facility-by-facility, so vendor revenue ramps depend on state budgets and FCC approvals.
insights.quote: The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.
insights.locator: The FCC approved the jamming order

insights.claim: Under the new FCC process, facilities wanting jamming must apply, describe deployment, prove via testing the signal stays inside the designated area, and notify nearby communities; the FCC is also seeking comment on closing loopholes on other frequencies and on quiet zones around prisons.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Testing and approval gates slow deployment; possible quiet zones could impose coverage constraints on carriers near prisons.
insights.locator: Chair touts plan to prevent interference

insights.claim: Carr cites estimates that as many as 500,000 US inmates have regular access to contraband cellphones used for scams, drug trafficking and violent attacks.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Sizes the problem driving demand for contraband-detection and jamming solutions.
insights.quote: as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices

insights.claim: Prison phone companies ViaPath (Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, plus prosecutor, corrections and police associations, supported authorizing contraband-phone jamming.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Incumbent prison-telecom providers benefit if contraband phones that compete with paid inmate calling are suppressed.
insights.locator: Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by

insights.claim: CTIA's pilot test with Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and the South Carolina Department of Corrections found micro-jammers blocked 911 calls and caused wireless infrastructure interference up to two and a half miles away, even with limited jammers, bands and power.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Collateral interference evidence is the core of any legal challenge and could constrain carrier network performance near prisons.
insights.quote: caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away
insights.locator: CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing

insights.claim: In CTIA's pilot, contraband devices in outdoor inmate recreation areas still completed calls in one-half to two-thirds of attempts, meaning jamming was simultaneously over- and under-inclusive.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Weak efficacy undermines the ROI case for jamming and favors alternative contraband-detection technologies.
insights.quote: current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once
insights.locator: CTIA said the pilot test shows

insights.claim: CTIA argues the FCC has no authority to allow jamming under the Communications Act, and the order could be challenged in court.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Litigation risk could delay or void the order; watch for a CTIA or carrier petition for review.
insights.quote: has no authority to allow jamming

insights.claim: AT&T argues the FCC's 'deauthorize subscriber operation' legal theory rests on a factual error because radio jammers block all communications on affected bands and cannot distinguish contraband from legitimate devices.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Carrier opposition signals the order will be contested on both legal and technical grounds.
insights.quote: There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others.
insights.locator: AT&T said the FCC’s legal justification

insights.claim: Commissioner Anna Gomez, the FCC's only Democrat, warns that introducing jamming equipment into the American market could fuel unauthorized sales and criminal use, citing Wi-Fi jammers already used to disable security systems and cameras in robberies.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Legalizing a jamming equipment market creates diversion risk that could prompt future enforcement or tighter rules.
insights.quote: the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise

insights.claim: Gomez partially dissented because the order does not bar prisons and prison phone companies from passing jamming costs into higher regulated inmate calling rates, since the FCC counts safety and security costs when setting rate caps.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Watch inmate-calling rate proceedings: jamming costs could become a lever for prison-telecom providers to seek higher caps.
insights.quote: it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures

insights.claim: Freedom of the Press Foundation's Seth Stern argued contraband phones have documented prison abuses, citing footage used in The Alabama Solution film and in a DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Civil-liberties opposition adds political and reputational friction to deployments.
insights.quote: Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country
insights.locator: Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy
